title: To become a better writer, read as much as you can
author: andsoitis
tldr: Science fiction author T. R. Napper says writing has no fixed method except one rule: read a lot, and widely. More of the aspiring writers in his workshops now say they're too busy to read, and he blames phone time for wearing down the sustained attention that reading and writing both need.

keyPoints: Napper tells his students there is no single blueprint for writing, with one exception. Read as much as you can, widely and well. Anyone who won't shouldn't be writing.

When he asks workshop students what they're reading, more of them now say they're too busy. His answer is to check your screen time, since two to seven hours a day on a phone is time you could spend reading. He writes full-time, works three gig jobs, has two children, and still reads every night.

Reading teaches craft without formal study. Early beta readers told him he had used three-act structure before he knew what that was. He calls creative writing classes and MFAs useful for some but secondary to reading.
Reading outside your genre feeds ideas. Hardboiled crime showed him where cyberpunk came from, non-fiction gives him raw material for stories, and poetry taught him word economy.

Citing Maryanne Wolf's 'Reader, Come Home', he argues that a phone-trained brain loses the sustained concentration reading builds, and that the reading brain is also the writing brain. Writing a book is a marathon and reading is the training. He reads 52 books a year and calls 20 the bare minimum.

He sees generative AI as a tool for people who like the idea of making art but don't like literature. He sets them aside and says a few weeks of reading for an hour a night instead of using the phone will start to rebuild the habit.
article.whyItMatters: Aspiring fiction writers who want the argument in the author's own blunt voice should read the original. The profanity and asides are part of what the thread fought over, and the summary flattens that tone.

comments.overview: Almost nobody disputed that writers need to read. The thread spent its energy on the qualifiers. The loudest pushback said practice matters more than reading, others said what you read matters more than how much, and many described their prose absorbing whatever they read. Side threads traded recommendations for prose-first novels, fought over the author's swearing, and drifted into a long, heated argument about whether a democracy needs a reading public.

themes.title: Reading is not a substitute for writing
themes.synthesis: The most common objection was that you get better at writing by writing, the way musicians practice an instrument and pool players drill one shot for hours. Lifelong readers said their writing still went rusty when they stopped writing, and one noted that advice to read a lot is far more common than advice to write a lot. Others answered that nobody proposed reading instead of writing. You need both, and the article's own footnote says writers must write. A few added that reading only pays off when it is deliberate, done to learn why a book works.

quotes.author: BeetleB
quotes.text: I've been reading a lot for decades. I'm a crappy writer. There is a saturation point.

quotes.author: presbyterian
quotes.text: You shouldn't read a lot *instead* of writing a lot, you should be doing both, in the same way a musician should practice their instrument *and* listen to a lot of music.

themes.title: People want to have written, not to write
themes.synthesis: Many explained non-reading writers as people after the status of author rather than the work. Commenters saw the same pattern elsewhere, in solo game developers who don't play games and ship unfun ones, founders in fields they don't care about, and musicians who stop listening and turn repetitive. Bobby McFerrin, who avoided other singers for a year or two to find his own voice, came up as a counterexample. A reply pointed out he already had a lifetime of listening behind him. Anne Lamott's 'Bird by Bird' was quoted on students who want to be published more than they want to write.

quotes.author: PaulRobinson
quotes.text: As the old quip goes: people don’t want to be writers, they want to have published a book.

quotes.author: cure_42
quotes.text: I see so many solo indie game developers who don't really play games and almost all of them fail to make their game actually fun.

themes.title: What you read matters more than how much
themes.synthesis: Several commenters rejected 'as much as you can' in favor of selective, critical reading. antirez suggested re-reading good books to see why they work and reading the odd bad one to see why it fails. A high school teacher's "garbage in, garbage out" was set against Faulkner's advice to read everything, trash included. Schopenhauer's line that not reading bad books is a precondition for reading good ones drew the reply that today's bad books are social media. The same question drove a long recommendation thread for prose-first novels, from Gene Wolfe, Mervyn Peake and Patrick O'Brian to Nabokov and Eco, where people argued over whether Pratchett's plain style counts as masterful.

quotes.author: antirez
quotes.text: Read *selected* books, and re-read good books more often then reading new stuff, to understand *why* they are good.

quotes.author: wyclif
quotes.text: You can't expect to read nothing but news, comic books, National Lampoon, MAD magazine (and in our era, blogs) and become a good writer. It just doesn't work that way.

themes.title: Your reading leaks into your prose
themes.synthesis: Commenters described picking up the voice of whatever they read. An engineer reading building codes started writing "shall" and "need not", heavy LLM users caught AI phrasings in their own speech, and one person's draft changed tone when they switched books halfway. Some took this as the reason to read good prose on purpose, as an antidote to office and HN jargon. Others found writing style harder to copy than musical style because its parts are hard to name. A reply listed them, from sentence length and complexity to signposting habits and personal quirks.

quotes.author: wcfrobert
quotes.text: Recently, I've been reading a lot of building codes and compliance documents and I've develop annoying ticks like using "shall", "need not", "take no exception", overuse of passive voice, etc.

quotes.author: d--b
quotes.text: If I change the book I read while writing something, my text changes tone in the middle.

themes.title: Phones, AI and lost attention
themes.synthesis: The screen-time argument drew the objection that phone time comes in 30-second scraps too short for a book. Replies cited Stephen King reading in ten-minute gaps and suggested leaving the phone at home with a paperback. A recent Atlantic piece on a 'postliterate age' anchored a debate over whether reading is now an individual edge or a social problem that individual habits can't fix. Several people tied the article's attention point to AI: they said reading model output bores them, and that since adopting coding agents they rarely or never reach flow state.

quotes.author: svara
quotes.text: It's a technique we must preserve for the good of our culture, but, also, in a society full of people who have forgotten how to, an individual superpower.

quotes.author: hrideshmg
quotes.text: One interesting thing I've just come to notice is that ever since I started using AI agents, ive not had a single moment of 'flow-state' whereas I used to semi-frequently have such experiences prior.

comments.consensus: Reading is necessary for writing well but not enough by itself. You also have to write a lot, and reading helps most when it is deliberate and of good material.
comments.dissent: A minority called the post gatekeeping. They said people who find reading hard may still have stories worth telling, that writers can find out for themselves whether reading matters, and that the "fuck you, you're not too busy" line was abuse rather than humor. Defenders replied that the joke targeted a stereotype, was retracted in the next sentence, and that a professional advising students is teaching, not gatekeeping.

contrarian.author: andersonl
contrarian.text: It is not obvious that the genre fiction writer is losing out by reading less compared to watching tv or movies. They would still be learning about pacing, dialogue, plot mechanics…
contrarian.why: It separates command of language from storytelling and argues that only the first depends on reading books, where the article treats both as one craft.
